strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of invariant learning: learning one stable predictive cue can leave a model vulnerable when that cue disappears. Encouraging alternative invariant cues is relevant to occlusion and robust visual recognition.

H-CMNIST provides a useful controlled diagnostic separating spurious-correlation robustness from reliance on an additional invariant cue. After removing color, ASGDRO improves Spu&Shape accuracy from GDRO’s 57.53±2.11% to 66.62±5.61%, supporting better exploitation of shape.

The evaluation covers subpopulation shifts, WILDS, and DomainBed. Reported improvements include CMNIST worst-group accuracy of 74.2% versus GDRO’s 68.6%, CelebA accuracy of 91.0% versus 87.2%, and DomainBed average accuracy of 74.0% versus 72.6% for DPLCLIP and 72.9% for DPLCLIP+GDRO. These results provide worthwhile evidence of practical utility.

Combining adaptive sharpness-aware training with group-robust weighting is straightforward and requires no annotations of individual invariant features. The appendix supplies substantial hyperparameter information, three-seed evaluations, and separate source-domain and oracle model-selection results for DomainBed.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false under its stated additive Euclidean perturbation constraint. In the setting of Appendix A.4, choose Y=1, Z=(1,...,1), and θ=λ with nonnegative weights summing to one. Then R(λ)=0 and max_{||ε||₂≤ρ} R(λ+ε)=pρ²/2 for every λ. A predictor using only one feature is therefore just as optimal as uniform weighting. The proof introduces an unjustified λ multiplier into the gradient norm and treats a first-order approximation as an equality. Consequently, the central guarantee that this objective favors diverse invariant mechanisms is not established.

The broader derivation connecting feature robustness to parameter flatness also lacks justification. Equation (4) equates a maximum over selected invariant mechanisms with a maximum over an entire parameter ball; containment supports an inequality, not that equality. Low risk along interpolation paths does not establish low risk throughout the ball. Proposition 1’s gradient-norm approximation likewise does not prove convergence to common flat minima, since zero gradients can occur at sharp minima. These gaps affect a principal claimed contribution beyond combining ASAM and GDRO.

The evaluated algorithm differs materially from the analyzed objective. Algorithm 1 and Equation (5) use environment-specific adversarial perturbations, whereas Section 4.3 states that all non-toy experiments use one perturbation computed from pooled empirical risk. That direction need not maximize any particular group’s loss, especially when group gradients disagree. No approximation analysis or direct comparison establishes that this substitution preserves the proposed mechanism.

The experiments support improved robustness more strongly than they establish SIL as defined. H-CMNIST is the only direct invariant-cue removal experiment; standard distribution-shift accuracy does not isolate robustness to missing invariant features. Larger Grad-CAM regions and smaller Hessian eigenvalues are suggestive but do not demonstrate multiple independently usable predictive cues. Comparisons with feature-diversity methods such as Bonsai and FeAT on the targeted H-CMNIST diagnostic would also help substantiate the claimed distinction.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for H-CMNIST splits and model selection, and Appendix A.8 provides WILDS results without corresponding detailed training configurations. These reporting limitations are secondary. The weak-reject recommendation is determined by the incorrect central theorem and the unvalidated connection between the analyzed objective, the implemented optimizer, and SIL, despite the useful empirical gains.
